title: Animated Steller's Jay, a beautiful AI benchmark
story_key: story|title:animated steller s jay a beautiful ai benchmark
content_excerpt: Steller - grady.dev Back Steller A fun benchmark, maxxed-out November 18, 2026 birds art ai See 6 interesting failures Everyone should build their own AI benchmarks. Why? Labs optimize their agents toward public benchmarks, so changes in benchmarks often overstate capability changes. What you want to use AIs for is often particular to you, and has quirks that don’t fit cleanly into a generic benchmark. Subjective benchmarks often give you a feel for the “texture” of quality that an agent produces, in a way that a benchmark that has to be reduced to a score/pass-fail cannot. Today’s benchmarks are comically overweighted toward coding and logic reasoning, just because they’re verifiable. Building your own benchmarks is fun, and adds a sense of excitment for new model releases. Thus, every time I hit a problem an AI agent can’t solve, or does a very poor job on, I copy the prompt down in a little file on my computer in ~/benchmarks/[NAME].md , sometimes with attached context like the files needed for the task. Then, when new models come out I run a few of them to quickly get a sense for what the new models are capable of. Steller One such (subjective) benchmark, which I’m now satisfied enough with the results of to call “passed” is STELLAR.md . Please create a detailed interactive environment in 3JS which features a single Stellar’s Jay, with the ability to have it move around (by both flying and hopping) in response to mouse clicks, and have it passively move around without human intervention, emulating the motion and passive activities of the animal. It should be in a simplified 3D scene that allows demonstration of the motion of the jay. Your goal is to capture in extreme visual fidelity the physical attributes of the animal, its modes of movement and patterns of behavior. Aim for realism, and avoid simplifications that would yield distracting visual artifacts. It should only use Javascript and HTML, and should work offline. You have access to run subagents through other models from other providers (via codex, claude, and agy CLIs) to check your work and provide visual critiques. You have 6h, and up to $100 in API credits to use (across all models). Any questions before you begin? I then answer any questions the model asks. A careful reader will realize in this prompt I type it “StellAr” (with an A), when it is in fact spelled “StellEr” (with an E) - something I learned while writing this blog post. I guess I’m not a great SPELLAR (lol). Progression I star

title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
summary: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

title: Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models
summary: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.

title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency
story_key: story|ver:27|title:daisyrose 27b pushing the frontier of post training efficiency
content_excerpt: Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. story_key: story|title:bot inator mac agent that writes its own tools runs them sandboxed
content_excerpt: Local-first macOS agent that watches what you do and offers to help. Nothing runs without your approval. A local-first macOS agent that watches what you do and offers to help. Nothing runs without your approval. Download for macOS (Apple Silicon, macOS 14 or later, signed and notarized) or build from source . It notices activity on your Mac (new files in Downloads, incoming mail and iMessages, upcoming meetings, app switches), asks an LLM "how could I help here?" , and offers an action, or a small tool it writes itself, as a card in the menu bar. bot-inator is not limited to the tools it ships with. When it spots something you keep doing by hand, or something you asked for in chat that it couldn't do, it offers to build a tool for it: Ways in besides the automatic offers: ask in Chat, or use Watch me to do a task once while it records the steps. The two talk over a WebSocket ( /ws/stream ) plus a small HTTP API. See ARCHITECTURE.md for diagrams and LIVING_SPEC.md for the full protocol and design history. The app is signed and notarized and carries its own daemon and Python, so it needs no terminal, Python or Xcode. It starts the daemon when it opens and stops it when it quits. Models are not in the download: with the local provider they download from the setup screen (about 12.7 GB). install.sh checks for macOS 14+, Apple Silicon, Python 3.11+ and the Xcode command line tools (it names anything missing), sets up the daemon's Python environment and builds the menu bar app. It is safe to run again. run.sh starts the daemon in that terminal (Ctrl-C stops it) and opens the app once the daemon answers. With the default local provider the first start downloads the models (about 12.7 GB, or 8 GB on a Mac under 24 GB); run.sh lists them first. It adds no login item: run it again after a restart. On the first start the app opens Set up bot-inator : it reads how much memory this Mac has, marks one choice "Recommended for this Mac", and waits for you to pick. No model downloads and nothing reaches a cloud provider before you choose. Change it later in Settings… (⌘,), then Restart Daemon . Provider setup, presets and model lists: docs/providers.md . Settings are saved to ~/.bot-inator/settings.json (readable only by you). They override .env , and variables exported in the daemon's shell override both. content_excerpt: Decks is a React slide framework for animated, data-driven talks, built to be written with coding agents. A deck is a directory of MDX slides and React components; slides are drawn on a 1920x1080 canvas that scales to any window, clicks step through motion inside a slide, and a story stage pins one visualization per slide and advances it in beats while a prose card carries the argument. It ships as one npm package, @steamfield/decks , with a decks command, and a Claude Code plugin that teaches an agent to build a good deck. Node 22.12 or later and React 19. The -p form keeps runners from fetching the unrelated decks package on npm. The user guide is docs/guide/ ; it also ships inside the package. Decks was a Slidev addon ( slidev-addon-decks ) until 1.0; the git tag slidev-final holds the last Slidev version of this repo.

title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
summary:
Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)

Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.

In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.

I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.

Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.

Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

title: External sandboxes for coding agents
summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
story_key: model:claude|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. >50% of tickets written by agents, the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR, and selling without SDRs or FDEs Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova , COO of Linear , about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation . We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app

title: Verifiable Logic in Medical LLMs: A Critical Review of Agentic Clinical Reasoning Optimization and Neuro-Symbolic Grounding
summary: Clinical large language models are usually judged by whether the final answer is right. Yet a model can reach a fluent, plausible output through invalid reasoning that static benchmarks do not detect, and confident hallucination, causally invalid inference, and spurious demographic shortcuts can pass conventional evaluation. This critical review covers four paradigms in turn: how clinical hallucination arises and why static metrics miss it; the agentic hallucination cascade, in which multi-agent and tool-augmented systems propagate and amplify early reasoning errors; process reward modeling as step-level supervision; and neuro-symbolic grounding, in which formal logic engines, ontology reasoners, and knowledge graphs place verifiable constraints on neural output. Within their encoded domains, systems with symbolic veto layers offer guarantees that hold relative to their encoded knowledge, and they report large gains on the safety measures they use. These results come from single studies, mostly in simulated or small-sample settings, and are not directly comparable with neural baselines. Process reward models remain bounded by the statistics of their training data. We propose a conceptual framework that maps each agentic failure mode to a symbolic intervention point, and we argue that clinical AI safety depends substantially on system architecture. Because current regulation emphasizes performance and does not require verification of reasoning steps, we argue that responsible certification should also audit reasoning trajectories alongside accuracy on static benchmarks.

title: DTS: Delta-Based Tile Scoring for Efficient Long-Context Sparse Attention
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly need to process long documents and codebases, making long-context attention a major prefill bottleneck. Block sparse attention reduces computation by skipping unimportant blocks of the attention matrix, but scoring blocks accurately can itself be expensive. We propose Delta-Based Tile Scoring (DTS), a training-free, content-adaptive tile scoring method for sparse block attention. DTS selects query and key anchors according to local vector changes, using fewer representatives in redundant regions while retaining more detail in heterogeneous regions. To accelerate anchor selection, parallel delta packing partitions the query and key sequences into tile-aligned chunks and performs bounded local scans over these chunks concurrently. The selected tiles are then computed using the original query, key, and value vectors. On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DTS keeps average RULER and LongBench scores within 0.10 percentage points of full attention, with RULER evaluated up to 128K tokens. At 128K tokens, DTS reduces measured scoring-pipeline latency by 38% compared with XAttention. On four NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it achieves a 3.3$\times$ prefill speedup over a PyTorch full-attention baseline using FlashAttention-2 at 512K tokens.

title: Why agent governance starts with observability
summary: A strong AI agent governance strategy
story_key: story|title:why agent governance starts with observability
content_excerpt: AI applications can range from simple internal chatbots to customer-facing, mission-critical agents, but all LLM-based solutions have the capacity to reason independently, so establishing governance has become a key consideration for any degree of AI adoption. Recent headlines on agent security breaches have driven even greater urgency to set up governance as a prerequisite for AI usage and development. While the need for agent governance is widely recognized in most organizations, most are still figuring out where to start. There is some top-down guidance on agent governance from governing bodies, such as the OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations , NIST AI Risk Management Framework , or AI Agents under EU Law . These guidelines outline agent risks, but don’t define how to mitigate these issues or verify that governance is working. When teams we work with are shipping agents with governing standards in place, we see two main strategies in common among them: Centralizing visibility across agents. Organizations need a central view of the agents running across the company, so costly operations, unauthorized usage, and rogue agents don't fall through the cracks. This visibility makes it possible to establish limits on agents and audit their behavior to verify that guardrails are upheld. Understanding individual agent behavior. Agents are non-deterministic, so the same agent can take different paths and call different tools on the same input. The issues that surface are often specific to each agent's task and execution path, so teams need access to the full trajectory of each agent run to understand its actions and alert on unexpected behavior. At the core of both of these strategies is agent observability , the ability to record, inspect, and analyze every step of your AI agent takes. This typically means tracing the steps and attributes of your agent, having the ability to query and access this data readily, and leveraging capabilities to interpret the agent behavior at scale. Observability is the cornerstone for governance strategies because a guardrail or spend/usage limit doesn't guarantee an agent will follow it, and agents need to be accurately monitored to verify that those guardrails work as intended. The metrics from observability then provide the data to continuously harden overall governance posture. We can think of agent governance methods at a company as either preventative or detective. title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
summary: New controls are now in LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data. Learn more.
story_key: story|title:protect sensitive data in your traces new controls in langsmith
content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. Debugging is handled with least privilege, so addressing performance issues like latency can be managed without exposing any sensitive data. If a customer reports an issue, you can grant access to only that customer’s inputs and outputs, and only to the people or teams required to address it. Everything is configurable through granular admin controls. LangSmith’s new input and output controls give admins greater control over what portions of a trace users can see. Trace inputs and outputs are where sensitive user data most often resides. Other trace data like run trees, performance stats, and metadata are critical for agent improvement and far less sensitive. With these controls, agent engineers can spot and resolve issues – like repetitive or slow tool calls – without seeing sensitive content, and those who need the full picture can be granted access as needed. title: claude-code v2.1.329
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a trust dialog warning that says where a folder's hooks are declared
  • Added a warning in the conversation, in Claude Desktop and other non-interactive hosts, when hooks in managed settings fail to load
  • Added this session's scheduled tasks, /loop wakeups, the goal and this conversation's forks to /tasks; x stops one after asking

  • Added a "Marketplace auto-update" row to /status that names managed marketplaces that get no automatic updates, and why
  • Added support for turning on Code Mode while OpenTelemetry events and metrics are enabled; each tool call the code makes sends its events; tracing still keeps it off
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json sometimes being reset to defaults when a network stall or file lock made it unreadable and cleared during a save
  • Fixed repeated sign-outs on macOS when Claude Code could read the Keychain but not save to it. That session now stops at expiry and says why, and other sessions stay signed in
  • Fixed /terminal-setup corrupting VS Code settings or keybindings files around block comments, and reporting success while losing the Shift+Enter binding where keybindings.json has an unclosed string
  • Fixed files accepted through the IDE diff being saved without their last newline, and losing their byte order mark (BOM) when an edit was accepted by saving the diff in VS Code
  • Fixed picking a cloud session in /teleport replacing your open conversation: the pick now starts a new session, as /clear does, and /resume brings the old one back
  • Fixed /usage-credits asking Pro and Max users to log in again after opening the browser, and the link disappearing after 8 seconds if the browser doesn't open and a task stops for usage credits
  • Fixed /usage saying usage credits are off when they had run out or reached the monthly limit, and /model not telling Pro and Max users when that limit blocks a model that runs on usage credits
  • Fixed the spend limit menu showing your spend as your monthly limit and wrapping its rows under the pointer in narrow windows
  • Fixed a status line script that prints without end freezing the prompt and using gigabytes of memory
  • Fixed an empty, frozen screen after approving managed settings while the --resume picker, the trust dialog or another set-up screen was waiting
  • Fixed choosing Default in /model replacing your saved model with your organization's default when the Default row already showed your saved model
  • Fixed an MCP server being signed in again after you cleared its authentication while a token refresh was running
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stalled after a slow reconnect: Claude Code now reconnects most HTTP MCP servers by itself when one is left on an older protocol version
  • Fixed PDFs, images and .docx, .xlsx or .pptx files that MCP servers or websites send as application/octet-stream being saved as .bin, which kept Claude from reading the PDFs and images
  • Fixed /code-review <pr number> sometimes reviewing the checked-out branch instead of the pull request without saying so: it now reads the pull request with gh pr diff, or says when it can't
  • Fixed /code-review stopping at a permission prompt, on most models, to look for a ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md that doesn't exist
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --push-outcome-on-release sometimes deleting a session's branch on the git host
  • Fixed Code Mode hiding a script's finished edits and the stopped command after Esc, and losing them on exit
  • Fixed a runaway loop in Code Mode filling the machine's memory; it is now stopped at a limit
  • Fixed a background agent running on when it was stopped while it was being resumed
  • Fixed background shell commands using memory for the earlier conversation until they exit
  • Fixed Remote Control using memory for the earlier conversation after a compaction or /clear in sessions run by Claude Desktop, IDEs or the SDK
  • Fixed Stop not ending a request in Claude Desktop sessions on Bedrock while it waits on a hung AWS credential_process or sign-in call
  • Fixed Claude sometimes failing to send you a file on its first try on Opus 4.8 and Opus 5
  • Fixed Claude not being told that a connected MCP server's tools could not be loaded, and taking it for a server with no tools, in sessions with tool search
  • Fixed claude mcp login and /mcp saying a service doesn't accept sign-ins from Claude Code when the service's client registration had been retired (HTTP 410 Gone)
  • Fixed another case of claude.ai-synced plugin hooks failing with "Plugin directory does not exist" while a session was still running on macOS
  • Fixed auto mode asking for manual approval to rm a symlink that points outside the working directory or at itself
  • Fixed /sandbox on Linux listing allowUnixSockets entries as allowed: they don't open those sockets there, and /sandbox now says so
  • Fixed pressing Esc twice to clear a mistyped code ending the sign-in in /install-github-app
  • Remote Control: Fixed sessions going back to their first effort level after a restart while the app still showed the level you picked (not yet for sessions that start in Ultracode)
  • Fixed a removed plugin's MCP server staying connected in headless sessions after reload_plugins or when the account's plugin list drops it
  • Fixed the Claude Docs connector's tools going missing when a plugin or MCP server at the same address failed to connect, and its error wrongly suggesting /login
  • Fixed a new skills, commands or agents folder being missed when --add-dir names the working directory or Claude Code starts in the home folder
  • Fixed sessions started from a pre-warmed process ignoring the autoCompactWindow setting in the project's .claude/settings.json
  • Fixed CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE staying in effect in a running session after it is removed from settings.json
  • Fixed the Agent tool's effort parameter being ignored for named teammates in agent teams
  • Fixed /auto-mode-setup ignoring recent auto mode denials when it scans a project for rules to suggest; it may now offer allow rules from them, and you review each before it's saved
  • Fixed a false "Couldn't save this change" warning after adding a permission rule or directory in a subfolder or worktree whose own .claude/settings.local.json is unreadable or malformed
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude to run a network proxy check after a failed request, which auto mode then blocked
  • Fixed headless rewind and fork going ahead while a message sent right after a model change still waited on it
  • Fixed Claude not being told when a background task was stopped while a cloud session was restarting
  • Fixed /team-onboarding reporting a guide as shared on Team and Enterprise plans when the server refused the upload
  • Fixed panels and questions being cut off at the prompt in fullscreen, /help, history search and the background tasks list losing rows or titles in short windows, and tables wrapping in dialogs
  • Fixed resumed sessions showing "Rejected" or "Declined" for edits, questions and plans that were cut off when the session ended
  • Fixed /passes showing the wrong number of passes after a server error, and offering usage credits for sharing when no guest passes are left
  • Fixed claude --help output being cut short when piped to another program
  • Fixed /terminal-setup turning on "Use Option as Meta key" in Terminal.app on macOS 27, and tips there suggesting Option+Enter instead of Shift+Enter
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed setup failing on Git LFS repositories cloned through Anthropic-managed git; sessions now start on pointer files, and git lfs pull fetches the content
  • Fixed sessions on self-hosted environments not starting from a git remote with an SSH host alias, GitHub SSH certificates or a GHE.com SSH user; an unresolved alias's error gives two git commands
  • Fixed remote MCP servers in self-hosted runner sessions staying without tools, or (over https) disconnected, after a timeout or network error
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as having stopped responding while Claude Code was still starting
  • Fixed Code Mode keeping in memory every large text file that code read, and memory growing each time a background subagent was woken
  • Fixed Code Mode stopping a script at its ten-minute limit while an MCP form, an MCP link prompt or a prompt that always asks was waiting for an answer
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts receiving a "moved to the background" message as data from most MCP calls over two minutes: the script now waits up to ten minutes, then gets an error
  • Fixed mods that list only some tools silently turning Code Mode off; such a mod no longer keeps it off, so use managed settings for that
  • Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn when the tool was called from a script that Claude waits for
  • Fixed a Code Mode script's let x; keeping the value that an earlier script gave x
  • Fixed a Code Mode script's call with no argument failing with a missing-parameter error on tools that need none
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts losing access to tools through tools in sessions with more than 4,096 tools
  • Fixed the /code-review findings card often showing "high" for a review that ran at medium, on most models
  • Fixed key hints in permission prompts, questions, /model and /rewind ignoring keybindings.json
  • Fixed auto-scroll, the PR status badge, the auto-compact warning and the ultracode tag not following the /config switches that control them in a running session
  • Fixed a custom cancel key not working in /add-dir, /tui feedback and the save-workflow form
  • Fixed arrow keys in the save-workflow form moving the selection in the workflow view behind it
  • Fixed /config saying nothing, or "dismissed", after changing many settings
  • Fixed Read and @-mentions showing one line too many for files that end in a newline
  • Fixed /status not naming the model that opusplan and haiku use in plan mode
  • Fixed claude doctor advising a Keychain unlock inside a macOS sandbox, where unlocking can't help
  • Fixed the "Jump to bottom" pill staying hidden after copying text and scrolling away, the row under it going blank when its label changed, and quick PageUp presses scrolling too far in fullscreen
  • Fixed a screen update sometimes being skipped when memory is low
  • Fixed long code blocks losing a blank line and repeating another in scrollback
  • Fixed prompt suggestions sometimes showing placeholder text such as _(no suggestion)_
  • Fixed the line about earlier messages on resume blaming a damaged file when the file was intact
  • Fixed characters disappearing from the prompt when its text held a color code that sets several styles and a keyword or command was highlighted
  • Fixed /rename and UserPromptSubmit hook titles in claude remote-control sessions not showing on claude.ai and mobile
  • Fixed the Remote Control diff listing a file twice when the branch renamed it and it was then edited
  • Improved the automatic clean-up of old sessions on computers with managed settings
  • Improved /tui and other in-place restarts to wait briefly for a login refresh, so they are less likely to sign you out
  • Improved memory use in long sessions that edit many files, and in long Claude Desktop sessions on macOS and Linux with many large MCP tool results
  • Windows: Improved start-up and the first search on PCs where Claude Code's search program starts slowly
  • Improved auto mode's handling of a short reply such as "yes" to Claude's question when telemetry is off, behind a gateway to the Anthropic API, or on Microsoft Foundry
  • Improved memory use of idle Claude Desktop and SDK sessions after a long turn, and after --resume or --continue of a session that holds screenshots or large tool results
  • Improved how fast a Claude Desktop Code session with Remote Control on is ready for the next message after an answer
  • Improved cloud sessions to retry plugins that failed to download at startup
  • Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a script makes thousands of tool calls
  • Improved Code Mode: after starting a subagent, Claude now gets the same guidance on waiting as outside Code Mode
  • Updated computer use on macOS to newer safety rules, so some actions are refused and some apps have less access
  • Changed saved scheduled tasks: in new signed-in sessions, most saved by earlier versions need scheduling again, though --resume of their own session still runs them
  • Changed /code-review with no target on most models to review the whole branch against the default branch, and fixed it losing the diff on multi-commit branches
  • Changed auto mode to run git status less often so most requests wait less in large repositories; a git command that discards changes may be blocked until the working tree is checked
  • Changed /code-review <pr number> --fix, and /code-review given a pull request URL, to stop without reviewing when gh pr diff is refused or fails
  • Changed 'Exit and stop tasks' to end this session's scheduled tasks so they don't run again on resume, unless you exit while Claude is responding
  • Changed some teammate panes to start through /bin/sh, so they may not read shell start-up files
  • Changed computer use on macOS to give up on an app launch that has not finished after 30 seconds

  • Changed Code Mode so a PreToolUse hook that errors no longer refuses a script's tool call, as outside Code Mode; set "onFailure": "block" on a command, HTTP or MCP tool hook that must refuse
  • Changed Code Mode to refuse a script's read of a line range over 256 MiB, which could use gigabytes of memory, and fixed reads of very long lines timing out
  • Changed Code Mode to also start when telemetry, nonessential traffic or feature flags are turned off; an administrator can keep it off in managed settings
  • Changed Code Mode to run a script that declares its own log, preview or sleep, which it used to refuse
  • Changed macOS login renewal to test the Keychain with a Claude Code-write-check item
  • Changed the /tasks header and the footer's background count to one number covering shells, monitors, MCP calls, agents, workflows and scheduled tasks
  • Changed Stop and SubagentStop hooks to list a Monitor's script as monitor, not shell, in background_tasks
  • Removed 2.1.326's automatic retry at the limit named in a max_tokens error; behind a gateway whose model takes fewer output tokens, set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS to that limit
  • [VSCode] Added a line above the message box after you decline the trust prompt, with Review trust to bring the prompt back without reloading the window
  • [VSCode] Fixed being signed out of Claude Code in every window and terminal when the sign-in server took 10 to 30 seconds to answer the extension's token refresh
  • [VSCode] Fixed keys pressed while an input method (IME) is composing moving focus on or declining a permission prompt, running menu rows and closing dialogs (#106358)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for Bash, Edit, Write and other built-in tools not showing why a safety check asks
  • [VSCode] Fixed a half-written plan comment being lost or moved to another passage, and an input method's Enter sending the comment, ending a session rename or picking an @-mentioned file
  • [VSCode] Fixed the limit banner not saying when usage credits are in use, and the session survey covering that banner and the usage credits card
  • [VSCode] Fixed screen readers not announcing a permission request that arrived while the Account & Usage dialog was open until that dialog was closed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a proposed-edit diff tab staying open, with an Accept button that did nothing, after its terminal Claude Code session disconnected
  • [VSCode] Fixed short tool inputs and outputs cut off at the panel's edge with no way to read the rest (they now open in an editor tab), and dragging to select text also opening one
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Up key putting an earlier message over text that an input method (IME) is composing in the message box (#101294)
  • [VSCode] Fixed dropping an Explorer folder onto the chat inserting nothing on VS Code 1.103 to 1.139 or in a floating chat window, and the drop highlight vanishing with a false "Hold Shift" hint
  • [VSCode] Fixed a permission prompt moving keyboard focus away from the details you were scrolling as its buttons switched on
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening in another editor group when claudeCode.lockEditorGroups is off (#108884)
  • [VSCode] Fixed ranges written with a single tilde (3~5 … 7~10) losing their tildes and showing struck-through text between them; only ~~text~~ is struck through now
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation errors wrapping into a narrow column, the spinner turning while a question card waits, and a NUL symbol after each letter in the output of a failed UTF-16 command
  • [VSCode] Changed Down to stop at the last item of a permission prompt instead of wrapping to Yes
  • [VSCode] Changed command output to show hidden characters and control sequences other than plain colors as symbols, so Persian, Khmer, Lao, Sinhala and Malayalam text can look broken or out of order

title: Genie 4 is now available
story_key: story|title:genie 4 is now available
content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. title: An updated Clairic and Clairic-flash are now open-weight, from the new Workers AI Superintelligence team
summary: Clairic graduates from preview, while Clairic-flash joins the repertoire on Workers AI. We’re doing an open-weight release for both extraction models.
story_key: story|variant:flash|title:an updated clairic and clairic flash are now open weight from the new workers ai
content_excerpt: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more. There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract .
